utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we resume the examination of the witness, I would like to give you the decision on a few issues that have been raised yesterday. First, I have no transcript on my screen. Yes, now I have the transcript on at least one screen, but not on my laptop computer yet. I think that it will function now, because my computer says computer -- yes, it's functioning. Thank you very much for the technical assistance. First of all, I would like to give you the decision of the Chamber which has been taken upon the suggestion of the Defence to organise the hearings in a different way. It was proposed by the Defence that we sit four days a week and three weeks a month. As I told you yesterday, the second suggestion is not followed by the Chamber, but suggestions have caused the Chamber to consider whether it would be in the interests of justice to change the schedule. I think there should be proper time to prepare the hearings, and our schedule is rather tight. So we slightly will change it. And the reasons -- the system we have in mind is that if we are sitting a whole week without any interruption by holidays or whatever, and if we would sit during that week in morning and afternoon sessions, we'll skip the Friday afternoon session. If we will sit the whole week without any interruption in long afternoon sessions, we will not continue on Friday until 7.00 but we'll stop at 4.30. If, however, we are sitting during the long morning sessions, the schedule will stay as it is. Let me just explain to you what this means for the weeks to come. The week starting on January 14th, there's no session scheduled Tuesday, the 15th, so there's no reason to skip anything during that week. The week of January the 21st we are sitting in morning and afternoon sessions, so on Friday, the 25th, we'll skip the afternoon session. The week of January 28th we are also sitting morning and afternoon. We'll skip the Friday, 1st of February, afternoon session. The week of February 4th there will be no -- there's no session scheduled on Friday, the 8th of February, so nothing will change in the schedule for that week. The week of February 11th we'll have morning and afternoon sessions. That means we'll skip the Friday afternoon session. That's Friday, the 15th of February. The week of February the 18th, no session has been scheduled for Friday, the 22nd, so nothing will change for that week. The week starting with February the 25th, we'll have long afternoon sessions during the whole week, so we'll stop at Friday, the 1st of March, at 4.30 in the afternoon. The same is valid for the week starting on the 4th of March. We'll stop on Friday, the 8th of March, at 4.30. The week starting on the 11th of March, there's no session scheduled for Friday, the 15th, so nothing will change in the schedule for that week. I just indicated to you what the system actually results in. Apart from this very practical decision, we also had to decide on the objections raised by the Defence against the admission in evidence of medical records used during the testimony of Dr. Nakas. First of all, the Chamber notes that there are no specific Rules on the authentication of documents in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Dr. Nakas has testified that he recognises the photocopies of the documents shown to him as photocopies of the medical documentation as they are kept in his hospital in Sarajevo in which he worked and that he was entitled to authenticate these kind of documents on behalf of the hospital. The Chamber accepts this as a sufficient authentication of these documents and therefore denies the objection of the Defence and admits these documents into evidence. The Chamber has taken into consideration that it has not been argued by the Defence that the documents were copies of forged originals, nor that there's any evidence that would support any suggestion that the originals would be forgeries. If the Defence, however, seeks to establish that either the content of these documents as unreliable they may present any evidence which would support this thesis. Similarly, it may present evidence or ask the Chamber to order further examination upon good cause shown in order to establish that the originals of the photocopies shown to Dr. Nakas were forgeries. Of course, this admission into evidence doesn't say anything about the probative value that these documents will have when evaluating the evidence later on. The Defence seems to have taken the position that forensic, non-destructive examination of medical records should be ordered or allowed as a matter of routine when such documents are tendered into evidence, and as a routine, I mean to say, as a routine once this has been requested by the party, so requested to have them forensically examined. The Defence has relied upon an unspecified decision in the Vasiljevic case. The Chamber has checked the Vasiljevic precedent and it could hardly be of any guidance to the Chamber since in this Vasiljevic case there were serious reasons to argue, and in fact it was argued, that the documents of which a copy was relied upon by the Defence to support an alibi Defence was a forgery, and the Chamber would like to have in the future clear references and sources to be given if a party relies on decisions taken in other cases. The Trial Chamber did find eight documents among which three orders related to the seizure and examination of medical records in the Vasiljevic case, and the Chamber thinks it would have been appropriate for the Defence to elaborate in further detail on the Vasiljevic decisions and to provide the Chamber with relevant information as to the content and the data, for example, dates of the decisions, if not even to provide the Chamber with copies of it, of what was presented as a relevant precedent. That's the decision as far as the admissibility of the medical records is concerned. I think that -- there was a final -- it has been suggested by the Defence that the Chamber should not admit the Prosecution to examine Mr. Ashton for the time it intends to examine him. The Chamber has considered the potential probative value and the relevance of the evidence and has decided that the Prosecution may proceed in the examination of Mr. Ashton. Then finally, I'd like to know whether the Defence was able to properly prepare the cross-examination also in view of the maps used by Mr. Ashton, so that we know where we stand. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President, for giving us the floor. I would just like to respond to one point. Before I respond to your question, I have to tell you that I will have to be absent on Monday. Unfortunately, I won't be able to attend the trial on Monday, which might cause certain problems, because it was my intention to cross-examine the witness. I still don't know how much time the Prosecution intends to examine the witness in chief. As to your question, unfortunately we have not been in a position, due to the lack of time, to elaborate entirely the documents. However, I note the possibility that you mentioned of having this witness brought back for additional examination. The Defence will be able to start the cross-examination tomorrow; however, should it be necessary, we hope that it would be possible to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: -- call the witness once again. We'll see in the afternoon how things proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you then call in Mr. Ashton, bring in Mr. Ashton, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just a minor matter in relation to the timetable. I notice that the most recent version of the timetable has us sitting on Friday, the 29th of March, which I think is Good Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I checked that and think a mistake has been made by the Registry, because Good Friday is a formal UN holiday, so I'll check whether we will sit or not, and the information given to me is that we will not sit on Good Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Blaxill: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may remind Mr. Ashton that he's still bound by the solemn declaration that he made at the beginning of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, if I may just remind you, as I shall remind myself, that we should watch the transcript carefully and not speed up as we are prone to do because we are working in our own native language. Mr. Ashton, at this time I would like, in fact, to put an album of photographs before you. We have supplied and served copies of these. They should be available to Your Honours. Mr. Ashton, I would like you, if you please, to look through that album, where you will see certain individual, small selections of photographs, and state to the Chamber whether you recognise those photographs, whether indeed you took them, and, very briefly, what the individual batches of photographs depict. So starting, if I may, the first batch of photographs we can identify with the ERN numbers or the concluding numbers of 1272 and 1273. Do you recognise those photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise these photographs. I took these photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, sorry. Could you wait until the print stops and then --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- start a response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These photographs were taken by me April of 1993, the first set, 1272 and 1273, while I was aboard a bus travelling through the city of Sarajevo. I got on the bus in front of the State Hospital, and when we reached one of the intersections that we discussed in testimony yesterday, where there had always been heavy sniping, a sniper fired into the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, I would ask: Perhaps when you start describing each photograph, could you just place the album onto the ELMO so it can come up on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the photo preceding 172, I took a picture -- or I actually had taken two or three pictures of people in the bus, and when we rounded the corner in the dangerous intersection, there was a pop and glass breaking and everyone went down to the floor. The bullet came in through the upper part of the window and when down into -- from this direction down into below the seat and out the side of the bus. It fired from a high angle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say whereabouts in Sarajevo was the bus at that time and where was the side of the bus facing that received the bullet hit?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bus was parallel to what would be Hrasno. Near Sarajevo but back towards Hrasno. The fire came from above the area of the sports stadium over in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left side of the bus -- sorry. The left side of the bus was facing the sports stadium as the bus was heading west towards the PTT from the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if we're going to have these location references, could the map be placed back in front of Mr. Ashton. And perhaps he could just briefly point out on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What map are we using now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: This would be the black and white, which is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The original, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I have the more detailed street map of Sarajevo that we used yesterday, or do we have one? This is a little bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If you're happy with that, Your Honours, I would be very happy for Mr. Ashton to use the larger-scale map that he used yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it has not been yet finally tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's your intention to have any markings made on it, it still could be done. I've got one problem. It's premarked in red.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At this time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this time. So I'd like to make a clear distinction on those premarks already on the map when it was presented to the witness, perhaps use exceptionally another colour if there would be any additional markings. I don't know whether we have any green.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, we could use blue if that would be suitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, blue could be used since black - I checked that - is for the Defence. So if the witness feels more comfortable with the small map, it can be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Your Honour. And if it's a convenient way to do it, Your Honour, perhaps we can use the marking "P" with a number for photograph or photographs, and then they can be P1, 2, 3, 4, 5 as we go through the individual sets of photographs in the album.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ashton, could you please mark on the map with the -- with "P1" where you say that incident took place that you photographed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to indicate, where do you say the direction of the shot came from? Could you just indicate it perhaps with an arrow pointing to P1, adjacent to it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the general direction from here to here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall who at that time held that territory?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That territory is in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I draw your attention now to the next set, the photographs, the second half of the ERN has been marked 1278 onwards to 1283. And again, could you just place that back on the ELMO. If you could thumb through the photographs on the ELMO, that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I explain this photograph, I'll put the map back to show where that photograph was taken as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular point is in the marketplace below Ciglane, below Kosevo Hospital and Ciglane, where I witnessed people going to get water every day. This area was a specific target at certain times of the day. There were no casualties at this time, but there were several people killed and wounded at this particular location getting water, by shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you take that particular photograph, Mr. Ashton?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was, I believe, July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken in Ciglane, when water was brought up for the local community, which is very close to the point where I just showed you the other picture but up on a hill in an apartment block right above it. This area was not deliberately targeted by Serb forces when people were collecting water because this particular water point was only occasional, as they tried to get tank trucks full of water and organise movement of distribution of water so it would be less dangerous to people to go out and collect water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when you took that particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also about the time of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same year, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken down on Marsala Tita Street, in the centre of town. Occasionally there would be water here but not every day, because the water supply was cut off in this area. This was about October here, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. This was October 1992. The next picture will identify the date for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you move to that next picture, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One moment and I will show you where this location is. This picture was taken right in this area here. There was a building here where the waterline came out, near the Presidency, just up the street from the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you mark that, then, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the marking "P2" sufficiently cover the area for all of those photographs in that batch?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative. I will have to -- I'll start with P2 up in Ciglane for the first photograph and I'll show everyone where Ciglane is. Underneath this road -- underneath this overpass here was a market, and right here, in this area here, which I'm going to mark "P2," was an area where people could collect water. This was an open area, easy to see from several of the Serb positions. Sniping occurred from up here, in that location, and shelling came in from various areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you move on, please, then to the other location that you were going to mark, and we'll go for P3 for that, I think. No. P2A, please, because it will keep within the batch.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be in the Ciglane apartment complex, the picture we looked at before, picture 79, which was right here, P2A. Then this picture, as marked -- as I showed the Court, on Marsala Tita.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Make that P2B, please, if you would.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This picture number 81 was taken at the same location. Picture 82 was taken at picture P2 position, at the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that particular photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: October 1992 I photographed this man, who I spoke to extensively, over a period of a few weeks. He was collecting water for people that couldn't get out of their apartments, other geriatrics who lived in the apartment complex near him. He was later killed by a shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in P2B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P2B. When did you take that particular photograph, Mr. Ashton?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, as regards the photographs taken in July of 1992 that you've referred to, did those water points remain at those locations after that date? In other words, were they still collecting water in those places in 1993 or beyond?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That location was a primary collection point for water. Water did not reach the city, but it reached certain points in the city when it was turned on, so people had to go to specific points to get the water, and that was one point where everyone had to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, the gentleman who appeared in the last of that particular group of photographs, did you remember any particular encounter with him in October of 1992, or a conversation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was a professor, retired professor, and we sat one day outside the Presidency, just down the street from P2, very close to that position, P2B, I'm sorry. And a shelling began in the area. People began running for cover and getting into doorways, and I got up and asked him to accompany me to safety of a nearby building, and he said to me that he was old and that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. Do you remember the exact words he said just as if in quotations? Can you remember his words?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall it right now. I just remember him telling me -- smiling at me and telling me that he was an old man and he didn't have any reason to fear or run or hide from this situation and that they would inevitably kill him anyway. He almost seemed to be able to forecast the future for himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton. Could we move to the next --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton. Could you move to the next batch of photographs, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1285. In the background you'll see the grain elevators for the bakery, where the bakery compound in Sarajevo was located. Every day people would line up outside this bakery to buy bread. The bakery was in plain view of the area above Grbavica. It was consistently targeted. There were a large number of casualties in this area. This particular incident, a shell landed close by the bakery and set a group of small shops ablaze. The fire department responded despite the fact the shells continued to come down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you take that photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I had better repeat, because I didn't have the microphone on. My question was, yes, when did you take the photograph? And I'm sorry, I didn't hear your response.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This incident was very close to the headquarters of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, United Nations Protection Force determined the shelling did come indeed from Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, on a subsequent occasion, have call to discuss that with anyone from the Bosnian Serb forces, from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular incident, no, I did not. In conversations with VRS soldiers, they admitted that they shelled certain areas of the city, but we didn't go into specifics about the bakery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not in respect of that particular occasion, did you ever discuss the bakery with Serb soldiers at any time, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did with one, but I can't remember what the conversation was about. We were talking about water lines, the bakery, the high number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1993, but I can't recollect exactly when that conversation took place. It was with someone in Grbavica, on the hill by the checkpoint, when I went to take some medicine to one of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to the next photograph, please. And that photograph is what, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same location that we just saw in the preceding photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same time, that is correct. October 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you turn the page, please. We've completed those photographs. Would you care to mark on the map with "P3" where that location is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now turn back to the photographs and move to the next, starting with the number 1292. And would you please tell us where that was and what date the photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was also very close to the bakery, same area of Novo Sarajevo, and it was in December of 1992. There was a mortar attack. I was riding in an UNPROFOR vehicle and asked to get out, because I saw that somebody on the steps was wounded. The shell exploded near our vehicle. We were coming from the angle that you see the photograph. We stopped at that point. I got out, made the photograph, saw that there was someone wounded on the front step of the building. I ran over to assist, after taking another photograph, and found a dead woman between the two vehicles that were burning, but could not recover her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the man and the woman wearing, in terms of clothing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were civilians. The man was an old man and the woman was a young woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you please now mark that one on the map as "P4."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, could you move to the next photograph. Is that a photograph of the same location and time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photograph of the same location, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move on to the next, please. Can you please tell us what those photographs depict.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Photograph 1300 is a picture of the State Hospital in December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what part of Sarajevo does that side of the hospital face?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That side faces Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you move to the next photograph. And what does that depict?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the rooms of the hospital. You look straight out over Grbavica. Trebevic would be -- Mount Trebevic would be to your left, the Jewish cemetery would be to your left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to that particular scene of damage, did you personally witness how that happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular impact, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps, then, move on to the next photograph. And can you say, as well, whether all these are contemporaneous photographs or taken at different times?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken at different times but within a few days of each other. They were very closely --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And over what period datewise would that be, roughly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: November -- October, November, December, in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was before more extensive damage was done to the hospital in later shellings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so I think at this point would you just like to move on through those photographs and just very briefly say what they depict.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each photograph depicts the damage to the side of the hospital facing Grbavica in these particular cases, where shells were fired, tank shells were fired into the hospital. That's the last one of the images I have here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time witness the source of damage of that type to the State Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on several occasions there were -- when I was in the hospital, this hospital was shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you actually witness the source of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to determine from where I was located in the hospital, in the fourth floor, at one point, that the shells were coming from a long distance away and striking the east side of the hospital, and again, one day when I was up on the 12th floor, the front of the hospital was hit, and I went down to a lower floor, and I could ascertain the next shell was fired, which went right past the hospital and hit the hill behind the hospital, was fired by a tank at the top of Grbavica, which I identified in yesterday's testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you ascertain that that was a tank firing from that location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was one of the first positions that I looked at through my camera lens when I went to try to find out where it was coming from. There were two places I would have looked. One was above the Jewish cemetery, where I had seen activity before, in that particular location. And when I looked through the camera lens, I had a telephoto lens on the camera, I saw tank in action. By the way, that was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other signs of gunfire, perhaps, say, at night or something, again when you were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Frequently I could see the flash, and we were hit by what appeared to be the 12-millimetre rounds, 50-calibre size round and they would come from different several different locations on hills above the Jewish cemetery from the top of the hill at Grbavica and some would come from lower positions down in Grbavica up towards the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say "frequently." Can you give any idea how often you saw that and during which sort of date period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In July of 1992, again October through December of 1992, and periodically throughout 1993/1994 and 1995, as late as 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton. Could you please move to the next batch of photographs. Oh, I'm sorry. Would you firstly mark that on the map with "P5."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] In the next series of photographs, 1319, you'll see a house on fire. The Jewish cemetery is visible in the lower -- in the upper left-hand corner of the picture. This particular incident I witnessed again from the same tank position early, around mid-afternoon, that the tank began firing from the top of the hill at Grbavica, near the monument, near the Partizan Monument. It was very clearly visible to the city of Sarajevo. It was out in the open. It continuously fired into that neighbourhood, striking that house and other houses around it. The house caught fire, and I photographed it for several hours as it burned. The following day I went to the community to see the damage for myself and met some of the citizens in the community, and they expressed anger because there was no military activity in that community at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see any incidents of tank fire from the location you described on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later that night, that same night, there was an exchange of fire. The tank fired down into that same area, but only higher up, along the edge of the Jewish cemetery, and at that point I saw tracers going back in the direction of the tank, but it was small-arms fire. And the tank fired five consecutive rounds very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did that happen, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us with any more specificity when you took the photograph that is in the album?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is around the 20th, 21st of September.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, yes. It was the day before, actually, two days before the shelling that brought so many wounded into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, did you, when you went to that location, did you look to see if there was indeed anything military near those houses?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Well, I didn't look specifically for any military presence, but when I arrived there was no -- I had been told that somewhere in the proximity of the Jewish cemetery was the Bosnian front lines. When I went past that area about 150 metres, I was stopped by a Bosnian soldier, who expressed to me that further up was the front line and I couldn't the go there, but it was not anywhere close to that house. And as I explained, the neighbours in that community expressed anger that that community has been shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we then move, if you please, to the map. Would you just make a mark where that location is, P5 - P6, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, actually, the actual street that I was driving on, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but I'm going to mark the approximate area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please move to the next photograph, the next set. Can you please describe that photograph and say where that is and when you took that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees on the first floor of the PTT when a barrage of heavy shells began striking in Novo Sarajevo. The attack went on for about 45 minutes. These were artillery rounds. They were not mortars, as they took a long time to arrive after the thump and the whistle coming in would indicate. I do not know the exact direction they came from, but this was one example of the so-called iron cross. They came up the street one by one by one, all way up to the PTT, and then sporadic shells left and right. And again, this pattern occurred three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that photograph taken, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give an indication of when in September?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to be after -- this was around the 23rd also, the 21st to the 28th of September, because I was out of Sarajevo and had just returned. That's why I was in that office that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss that with any contact of yours on the Serb side, as it were?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, as I mentioned in yesterday's testimony, I had spoken to Indic about this, but it was this particular incident that I brought up with the Serb logistics officer in Rhein-Main, who introduced me to this term, the iron cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now, then, please, mark the map with the location that you photographed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please do that on the ELMO so that we can follow it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is P7?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, P7.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Can you see -- yes, you can see it here. I've marked all the way from here to here, was the general area of the main attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, could you move to the next photograph, please. I think it will be number 1352 and 1353.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were casualties in this attack, by the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you wish to describe -- you mean, you mentioned casualties. Can you give an indication of numbers, and were these civilian casualties or military people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were civilians walking on that boulevard on the main street there. They were taken to State Hospital. Three of them were taken to State Hospital and two, I heard, were taken to Kosevo Hospital. The State Hospital casualties were minor wounds, the Kosevo Hospital casualties were serious wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton. Would you move on to the next photograph set, please, which I believe is 1352 and 1353?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. 1353 does not follow 1352, as you've just indicated. The next one is 1389, as far as I can see. That's also how it is indicated on the first page of this series.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry. It is 1352 and 1389. I'm sorry. That is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ashton. Could you please state what is depicted in that next set of two photographs and say also when those photographs were taken.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It's not on the screen, but 1352, 1389, and 1392 were all taken on September 25th, 1992. This is the morning I described in yesterday's testimony as the morning the hospital was shelled. The area outside the hospital was heavily shelled from the Presidency up to Tito barracks. There were as many as 40 casualties brought into the State Hospital and others taken up to Kosevo Hospital. One of the victims in this picture, Sandra, she was brought into the emergency room. I spoke to her. She spoke English. When she told me that she and her boyfriend went out to help a woman wounded by the first shell, there was a brief pause and then the second shell exploded, wounding both of them. She remembered the explosion, but she didn't remember anything after that. Her boyfriend, Svetozar, was pictured in photograph 1392, expressed to me that he held her hand as they laid on the ground and thought that this would be the end, that they were going to die, but they were rescued by a Bosnian policeman and brought to the hospital. I interviewed several of the patients that were less seriously wounded, to find out that they had been waiting for a bus and a shell landed right in the area of the crowd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, were these people civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move -- would you please mark that as "P8" and then move to the next photographic entry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Since I was not where the victims were wounded, and this was taken in the State Hospital, we already have that marked on the map. Do you still want me to mark P8 next to that or just use the same --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, as we have already to State Hospital --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please move on to the next photographs, if you would.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This young man, Mirza, was brought into the hospital on September 22nd, the day before Sandra arrived. He was brought in around 4.00 in the afternoon. It was a clear day, bright day. He and a group of other children were playing in Novo grad, in Alipasino Polje, a section of Sarajevo, which I will go ahead and mark on the map as "P8."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how old was the young man in question?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nine years old, I believe, or ten. I can't recall exactly here. His father was a former diplomat. He was playing with some other children, a group of children, and there was another group of children about ten to fifteen metres away from them. The father was only a few metres from him. His uncle was a few more metres from him when the shell landed. The kids were all playing, he said. There was laughter, they were joking, and suddenly there was this terrific bang and silence as he recounted the incident. When he was brought in, he was conscious and talking but he went into a deep state of shock because he lost a lot of blood from his leg wound. There was a young girl about 6 years old who I started treating. She had a hole in her arm. She didn't speak any English, but to my surprise, Mirza spoke fluent English. And I was able to learn more about the incident after -- two days later, after he was on the road to recovery. However, at this time the city had been shut off by the Bosnian Serbs. The medical supplies could not get into the city. The airport was being held up. The UN could not get the supplies in. Antibiotics were not available at the hospital and because we didn't have antibiotics for post-surgical procedures, the next morning the boy got a serious infection in the leg and we amputated the leg the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you take that photograph? Was that in State Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was taken in the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you move, then, to the next photo set, Mr. Ashton. Can you say again where and when that photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was also taken at the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that, I believe, is photograph -- would the ERN number that ends 1375; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything further about that particular person?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She was in her home when the shell struck the house. There was a fire, and also she found that when she tried to get out she couldn't move. But she was rescued. She had lost her leg. She had considerable damage and what was left had to be cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to move, please, to the next photograph. I believe the number is 1376. Can you say when and where that was taken?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This again was October 1992, at Kosevo Hospital centre, in the Pediatric ward, one of dozens of children wounded in the ward. She was playing and a shell landed and severed her spinal cord.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ascertain how old --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether she recovered from that injury?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: She had serious health problems due to the injury, and she was paralysed for life, but she did eventually leave the hospital after several months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you ascertain that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited the hospital regularly, and especially in the pediatric ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you move, please, to the next photograph, 1383 -- I'm sorry. 1384. I'm sorry, 1383.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph is in the State Hospital. This victim was brought in in the early evening. He had been shot by a sniper near the Presidency. He died about 15 minutes into this procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain if he was a civilian person or a military person?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a civilian. He was on his way home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the date of that photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to move to the photograph 1384.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken near the end of September of 1992 or the first few days of October 1992. It was early in the morning. I went up to Kosevo Hospital centre about 9.00, and he had been shot two times, once after he fell, one bullet went through his hand and completely severed his hand. There was a shell blast, and a witness said it was the shell that did the damage, but he claimed it was the bullet, so I couldn't determine what caused the -- but it was -- there were incidents going on of sniping and shelling at the same time that this particular man was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ascertain where the wounds were allegedly sustained? Whereabouts was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not very far from the hospital centre, but I don't know exactly where he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you manage to find out what he had been doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a worker, city worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A city worker. By that, do you mean it was a civilian person?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a civilian person. He was doing maintenance work or cleaning work of some kind, he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you've made reference to the hospital. Does that mean he was near Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was very close to Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we move to the next photograph, 1385, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you want me to mark Kosevo Hospital centre on this map, by the way?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take the next number? I think it's P --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- 9, and just mark Kosevo Hospital for us.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] This is 1385; correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in October of 1992. There had been a shelling near the Tito barracks, where this woman was running across the street. A mortar shell or artillery shell landed. I was not aware of the type of shell because I was not at that incident. I could hear the thumps near the hospital, and she was brought in moments later after the shelling began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from what you're saying, do we assume that photo was taken at State Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was taken at State Hospital, and she said she was wounded crossing the street next to Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given sufficient information -- sorry. Were you able to know enough of the location to be able to mark the map?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please do so, "P10."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the final photograph, if you please, 1388. Can you describe when that was taken and circumstances it depicts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of September, 1992, when the heavy shelling took place outside the hospital and the shells had hit the hospital, these victims were brought in. It is the woman who is lying here with her face covered who told me that they were waiting for a bus. She gave me a detailed description of the situation, told me that several people who were in the room, in this emergency room around her, were wounded at the same time. As I said, we had over 40 casualties at this time from this particular shelling. We had victims in this particular incident lined up in the hall and in other rooms, because we didn't have enough medical staff to do triage. One woman was brought in in such bad condition. She was moved aside, where she died, where I witnessed her death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of that number of people, are you aware of the number of fatalities and the number of injured, the ratio in that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the incident, I can't recall right now the number of fatalities in that -- I recorded that in my journal, but I believe there were three, at least three, that I knew of. One, as I said, I witnessed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were people waiting for a bus on that date. Does that bear relation to the photograph 1352, the lady named, you called Sandra Putic, I believe, or a name like it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was that same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same time, within 15 minutes, we received all of these casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just finally, you've made reference to the hospital. Would you just confirm which hospital that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is State Hospital, and before you proceed, I would like to go back to one picture and add information on Mirza's picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do, Mr. Ashton. Are you referring to photograph 1354?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1354 and 1355. I was beginning to mention that Mirza's uncle and father were standing nearby. I described the little girl was wounded, and other children were wounded. We had a 7-year-old boy come in from this particular shelling. But Mirza was laying on the gurney conscious when he came in, and his father was brought in, completely mutilated on a stretcher. The boy saw it. And this is when he deteriorated very quickly, and of course because of blood loss he went into a state of shock as well. But his uncle was killed also in this shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That concludes my questions relating to the photographs. Thank you. I have one very quick topic which will fit before 11.00, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will conclude your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will have one further topic after the break, if I may, and it will not be for long, I promise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be possible to have the break a bit later, perhaps, and continue -- I don't know how much time it would take. If we would finish, say, at 5 minutes past 11.00, if that would conclude --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That wouldn't take me to the finish of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you may cover the topic you have in mind at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I would appreciate the break for my throat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, there's just one point I would like to bring up with you, and that is this: On your visits to the office of Major Indic in Lukavica, did you ever observe the presence of receiving equipment for broadcasts or the presence of television sets, either in the office or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see a satellite -- a series of satellite antennas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were they located?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside, to the left side of the entrance of the building where Indic's office was located. There were television sets in the office. At one time there was CNN. I do not know if it was a video recording or if it was live satellite feed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when you saw this CNN on the television?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sometime in 1993. To be precise, I could not pinpoint it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss, as it were, media coverage of anything with Indic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of times, because he knew that formerly I had been a photo journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Major Indic give any indication to you that he was aware of media broadcasts regarding events in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was aware, and there were two sides to this, in his view. One was that the Serbs had been improperly represented by the media, but on the other hand, he welcomed the media to come and film on their side. As I know, Christiane Amanpour from CNN interviewed General Galic on more than one occasion and interviewed people in Lukavica barracks as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton. Do you recall the piece of CNN broadcast or tape that you saw, do you recall what it was about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not involving Sarajevo; it was involving -- it was just a general news broadcast. I wasn't paying much attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That concludes the topic, Your Honours, so we are just approaching 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before we bring in the witness, if I can address the Court, please. I just have a practical suggestion for the future. From now on, we will be referring ourselves frequently to the exhibits. In order to avoid mistakes, could the registrar perhaps give the parties, after each hearing, a list on the current state of exhibits so that we could orient ourselves without difficulty? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would like to comment on that? Because as far as I understand, quite frequently such lists will be distributed. I don't know whether it should be on an every-day basis, but could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe my colleagues already stressed at the TMM meeting that normally we distribute this list every two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's any specific need, meanwhile, to have it more frequently, you can apply for it. So if there are specific reasons for that. But as a basis, I would say we stick to the scheme as indicated by the Registry. Thank you. Mr. Blaxill, you then may proceed after the witness has been brought in. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. Ashton, you will perhaps recall that I made reference to, as it were, the psychological effects on the civilians in Sarajevo of the shelling and sniping. So do you recall someone by the name of Vanessa, Vanessa, I believe, Dusejo or a name like that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall ever having a specific conversation with her on that subject?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I had several conversations with her on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was she?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a medical student, the daughter of a doctor at one of the hospitals in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having such conversations with her, do you recall any particular words she may have used describing her feelings on that subject?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I first met Vanessa, she was 19 years old at the time and working as a volunteer in the hospital. She told me that she had hoped that the Serbs would put down their weapons and come back to Sarajevo. She expressed that many of the young people of Sarajevo didn't believe this was happening and that they would forgive the Serbs if they would come back and try to work out some kind of a government where everyone would live together in a democracy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she offer -- sorry. Did she offer any comment as to her reactions to the sniping or the shelling of the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later she did. She was in a state of shock about it, of course. It was very, very difficult for her. Again, I mean, I was very surprised that she said she could forgive. But as time went on, her reaction changed, like so many other young people that I talked to there, she had the very same psychological changes that came with long-term exposure to trauma and violence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, though, any specific remarks she made to you as to her feelings about, say, the sniping, the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To terrorize and humiliate the population. She was very specific about that. She felt that this was a way that the Serbs were trying to get their point across.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the words that she actually to you used at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now the comment. I do have -- that was in one of my journals, because I wrote down remarks that she and others made at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about when was that conversation you had with her on that subject?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first conversation, in reference to laying down the weapons and coming back, if the Serbs would just lay down their weapons and come back, and the forgiveness was early. That was in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The later conversations, particularly on the subject of sniping and things of that nature, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: October, November, in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any such conversations with her after that date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, if I may intervene. No year was mentioned,, not in respect of July, October, November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: My omission. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: July 1992, in reference to the first statement, and in reference to her later statements, October, November 1992 as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any such kind of conversations with her or with other people during the course of 1993 and the first half of 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With several people, and the results were much the same from different people that this was active terrorism, it was an act of horror. They wanted to horrify the people, they wanted to destroy us. They specifically pointed out that they were civilians. They had nothing to do with this war, they wanted nothing to do with this war. This was a consistent conversation I had with many people. It was the same conversation over and over and over again. People questioned why, and why the International Community was not helping or intervening, because there were so many civilians being killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any kind of -- could you assess the level -- you've used the word "terror." What sort of level of fear, personal fear, did people express to you as time went by?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they all felt that at some point they were going to be killed. They felt that there was no hope. All hope had been given up for a lot of the people there, and there was just a sense of complete abandonment. And the psychology of the people was one of deep depression, animosity, not just towards the Serbs but towards the world, for not helping them. There were people there who threatened suicide to me and to other UN officials at UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, you've referred to threatened suicide. Did you have any knowledge of what the suicide rate was in the city or whether it varied during the course of late 1992 and through 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be perfectly frank about the suicide rate, it was very difficult to ascertain a figure or a general idea. The problem is the hospitals reported that people were increasingly committing suicide. I didn't see anyone in particular who did it, but I heard people threaten to do it. But the problem that I did see was people that I encountered every day or two and talked to in the streets, slowing down, I asked them, "Why aren't you protecting yourself?" And they were saying, "There's no reason to run, because you're going to die." There was a complete change of attitude of self-preservation. That deteriorated, and you could see that very clearly. That was not something that was there when I first arrived, the first year practically. It was within a year the whole scenario changed with everyone that I knew that was local and who could not get out of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any particular physical effects that were manifest in the people as they were living under these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Increased demand for alcohol, a demand for narcotic drugs, to help them through the day. There was a problem, obviously, of food shortages, because the Serbs constantly cut the city off from the airport, cut the UN convoys off, so there was a very small amount of food for most people. And people were suffering from malnutrition. Many people, especially geriatrics that I talked to, because I visited many, many apartments where people were identified to me, in my organisation, who could not get out or were afraid to get out. When we took medicine to these people, they told us they were too frightened to go out and some of them had not been out in a month, and if someone who they knew or a relative had been killed or wounded, they would be in the apartment for a period of two or three weeks at a time with nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the attitude of parents towards their children and the safety of their children?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first the parents were very, very cautious of children. I saw a lot of children in Novo Sarajevo playing in the streets, but as soon as a shell would land, the children would be herded in, parents would run out, pull the kids in. But they weren't allowed to play outside so much. However, later on there were more and more children outside. But the children became very hostile. They were very -- they constantly -- the boys started to play war, the girls started to become very frightened and intimidated. And I talked to some young children who told me that they were -- couldn't live confined in their homes any more. Many of them had seen mates die or wounded, and they were scared they were going to die. They were very frightened they were going to die. And I heard many comments that would normally be made by an adult made by children as young as 6 and 7 years old about the international community not doing anything to help. These are conditions indicative to trauma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, I just have two or three minor points now to ask you, if I may. Firstly, did you have contact with the civil protection people within Sarajevo who did that work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer me just one question in respect of those people: Were those people ever observed by you to be carrying arms or appear to be in military equipment and apparel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any of the civil protection units carrying arms. I encountered them at certain checkpoints throughout the city. I conferred with them. There were often Sarajevo city police officers who I got to know quite well and visited their police headquarters in different locations of the city who had occasionally a sidearm or an AK-47, but the civil personnel did not carry weapons that I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The next question I have is: In relation to the types of -- you've referred to certain ammunition used. Was ever there any kind of ammunition that had an incendiary effect or a light-giving effect when it was fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On only a few occasions that I witnessed incendiary shells were fired into apartment blocks in the centre of Sarajevo and in Trg Heroje section of the city, when firemen attempted to extinguish these fires, they could not do it. The shells would continue to burn with water, but when the shells struck, they sent out a large plume of bright white smoke and flaming debris, and the intensity of light within the area of the shell impact lasted for quite some time consistent with phosphorus shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say on a few occasions you witnessed these. Can you tell me when those occasions were, the month and the year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: September, October, December of 1993. And I believe I saw an incident in July, but I can't recall exactly if it was in that area or the September area. But it was still warm then. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By July, do you mean -- which year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these dates were in 1992. I did not see any --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I stop you one moment, sir? You previously responded "September, October, December of 1993."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correction. It was 1992. I did not see any of these incidents in 1993. I saw them in late 1992, during the time of October -- December, October, November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, I've asked you about access to the media in Lukavica. Did you ever visit or observe any media presence in Pale when you were visiting there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a media centre there. I went to visit it once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how effective did you consider that to be? What was there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The woman I met there was very polite. She said that journalists frequently came, and she was more than willing to assist and give the history of the Serb Republic from their point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, with your experience of the media world, consider that it was -- it appeared effective and gave them good access to media reporting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It seemed -- hold on. It seemed that they had a well-organised media centre, and they gave access to journalists who wanted it. There were some fears in Sarajevo among the journalists that Serbs would mistreat the journalist, but as some international journalists went to Pale, they found that their treatment was hospitable, but they would complain a lot about just being subjected to propaganda, but that was all that I ever heard from journalists who I talked to from ABC News, Sky News, CNN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, if I can turn your attention now to one feature on the map on which you placed a number of markings and your original comments. There is a marking in blue, a dotted blue line. Could you just explain to the Chamber, please, what that represents.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dotted blue line is the line that I frequently travelled on a daily basis into and out of the city of Sarajevo to Lukavica, to Pale, to Grbavica, and to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one final question, please, Mr. Ashton. You started your evidence informing the Chamber of your experiences of a number of war zones or conflicts. From your experiences, can you offer a final comment to the Chamber that compares what you witnessed in Sarajevo and its impact on civilians with what you witnessed in those other conflicts and the impact on the civilians there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unfortunate reality is that everywhere I have been, in Lebanon, Ethiopia, Morocco, Algeria, Afghanistan, civilians have had terrible trauma because of the conflicts, but the majority of conflicts that I visited were not conflicts where civilians were deliberately targeted on a daily basis. In the case of the countries I've previously mentioned, before I arrived in Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia, civilians were pretty much free to move, free to come, free to leave. In the case of Yugoslavia, immediately I was aware in Croatia and Bosnia of the intense destruction of civilians, civilian targets, the deliberate destruction of individual homes belonging to one ethnic group or another, which I did not see in other conflicts. The level of violence towards civilians in Bosnia, particularly in Sarajevo and other areas of Bosnia I visited, was, in my opinion, beyond reason, beyond belief for me, and for many of my media colleagues, before I became a humanitarian, I talked to many journalists about this, and we were all shocked by the amount of civilian damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton. Your Honours, I thank you, particularly for the indulgence and time. That concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. I'd like to give my colleagues -- before I give the opportunity to the Defence to cross-examine the witness, are there any questions at this moment to be put? I would like to put one question to you at this very moment, Mr. Ashton. During your testimony, you were asked about your conversation with Major Indic, and you mentioned that you once put a question to him: Why did you allow this to happen? And for one reason or another, finally no answer was given by you on that issue. Could you please inform the Chamber about the answer given by Major Indic on that question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indic responded with the answer that somewhat shocked me. It was that the Muslims had to learn that they were under the Serb domination and that the Serbs were the superior force in this area. He went on to tell me that if they really wanted peace, they would lay down their weapons and allow the government of Radovan Karadzic to return to Sarajevo. That's the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We discussed yesterday that you would have a combined cross-examination. Whom will start? Mr. Piletta-Zanin or Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to start, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ashton, if you allow me, I would like to start out in French. First of all, thank you for coming here. You have told us, the day before yesterday, I believe it was, that you had started your training as military in the US Coast Guard.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe -- yes, I was just going to ask you to confirm this. Is this exact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe I heard you say that you had worked there as a military staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify that question and tell me where you're referring to? You mean the Coast Guard or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to try and be ever more clear. You did declare that in June 1993 -- 1973, sorry, that you started on that first job, and was it as military?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The US Coast Guard at that time was under the Department of Transportation of the United States government. However, during wartime the Coast Guard is under the United States Department of defence. At the time I went into the Coast Guard during the Vietnam War, the Coast Guard remained under the Department of Transportation, but we were trained militarily by the Department of Defence because the Coast Guard maintained the river patrol sector of the Vietnam rivers. The Coast Guard was a major participant in the conflict in Vietnam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't heard your answer. So you were a military person; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically, no. I was a member of the Department of Transportation and technically yes, I was a member of the military because we were trained as military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So am I correct to assume that your answer is yes and no?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have told us that you have gone through university training as well, more specifically, political history courses, I believe, as well as the history of religions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your capacity as a historian, could you tell the Court when the peace treaty ending the Vietnam War was signed, where, and who were the parties to that agreement?
