utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact the five were not carrying weapons, you can ascertain that they were all off duty, I suppose. There were some HVO soldiers travelling with us, and there were HVO soldiers in the area, two of which were right in front of me, and they were dressed in uniform and armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, did you use the term "to escort," the word "escort"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because when you go in an area that you don't know in Sarajevo, you ask anyone to escort you, locals, anybody who knows the area, where the risks are, where the dangers are, so they can at least tell you who is who and what's going to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those five police officers who were not wearing uniform, were they escorted by two members of the military?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were friends of my -- my friend Sane, who I was with, who brought me out from Sarajevo who was an off-duty police officer. He met them in the street. We were all talking. When we went to the front lines, we were talking to soldiers wearing HVO uniforms. They escort us all the down the trench line until we crossed the street, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And may we be told what was the reason for them being with you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two of them had family members in the apartment blocks in Otes across the street that we were going to. One of them wanted to take me to meet his parents. I don't know -- the other two were friends of theirs. They were all together when we arrived and talking, so I have no reason -- no knowledge of why they would have accompanied us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were injured, sir, wounded by a bullet, would it be correct to say that it was somehow between the two front lines or very close to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the front lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that from a hill near Sarajevo, the Serb side was capable of identifying people, recognising them on the basis of their faces, and thus know who they were. Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I then wrong in saying that we might then think that in the course of that incident, accident that I was referring to earlier on, that the Serb side might have been in a position to recognise someone amongst your escorts and recognise them as military staff or policemen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the question that you've just referred to earlier was about Trebevic. It had nothing to do with this particular area, or this incident. However, I have no clue why a Serb would fire at anyone. I was the first target. They wouldn't shoot at anybody else. I was the first person that was shot at. So I wouldn't have an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would now like to go back to the matter of hospitals. You worked for a sufficiently long time at hospitals to know about the way in which the morgues were operated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sufficiently long time, yes. To know about the way the morgues were operated, I didn't spend time in the morgue. I visited the morgue and took pictures in the morgue of dead people when were brought in, wounded women and children, but I didn't spend any time there talking to the operators of the morgues, the director of the morgues, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your knowledge of the inside of that area, what happened to the corpses once they had been introduced and then left at the morgue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Corpses were brought in to the morgue either from the street or the hospital. Generally they were taken first into the hospital emergency room and then brought over to the morgue. The bodies were placed on gurneys or on what tables were available, and if there was an overflow of bodies, they were placed into caskets, which there often was. Many older people had no family left in Sarajevo so they left for someone to come and identify, but since they had no relatives or survivors, they were left there for quite some time and then buried in the Lion's Cemetery or other cemeteries around the city of Sarajevo. I don't know the length of time a body was left, although I did see some for three, four and five days waiting for someone to come and identify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to sum up, and you could agree with me in saying that after a certain period of time the bodies were taken directly to the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as I was told by one of the -- at the morgue at Kosevo, the fellow who handled the bodies, he said they waited ample time, which is generally five days. Usually someone would come within a day or two, if a relative didn't show up at home or the Bosnian government knew who it was. Often they had papers with them, but even so, sometimes a relative couldn't be found so the body was buried after a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this stage I would like to submit two photos to the witness. I would like to specify that those pictures come from the Prosecution. We've copied them and we've got them in a file. We've got seven copies of each, and so perhaps we could give them to the registrar as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to put any question concerning one of the photographs? Please indicate the number of the photo and put your question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this comes from the same document that you have in front of you, 0039137300391373.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were in an initial binder that we had received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to show a photo to the witness which was not been shown before, you should have it either marked for identification or you have to tender it into evidence. You can't just give numbers of -- we have no access to any other documentation apart from that which has been given to us in this court. So if it's in the binder, we can just put it in front of the witness. If not, you have to follow the procedures we earlier discussed about marking for identification or tendering into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As a matter of fact, it will be D10 and D11 for the two pictures. I do apologise to the Court, but we had to prepare in haste, for the reasons that you are familiar with, and so it was simply not possible for us to deal with everything at the same time. Since we have received important documents a couple of moments beforehand. So the numbers will be D10 and D11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and also the witness with the prenumbered document which you intend to tender into evidence and which is a photo. Mr. Usher, would you please. Please -- has the witness got the photos? If you would please put them on the ELMO. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which picture do you want first on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin will guide you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, a question which will refer to both photos at the same time, because generally speaking, at first sight, I would just like to know whether these are the pictures that you yourself have taken, both of them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, these are the two pictures that I took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please look at the photo where the final number is 73, the last two digits with 73.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you took this picture at the Kosevo Hospital morgue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you specify, sir, on what date this photo was taken?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was taken in the middle of July, as far as I can recollect from this photo. I took some in October and September, but I can't recollect the exact date this particular photograph was taken, but I believe this was July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific as to the date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even not if it concerns the year, Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other hand, as to the location, you are absolutely certain of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Kosevo morgue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you now to look at the other picture, D11, at the last two digits are 59, 59 -- 58, sorry, 58.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe what we can see here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see the body of one woman and one man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have the negatives of these two pictures?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the slides. They are in positive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that if we compare these two photos, the one that you have in front of you, where the final number is 58, and the previous one, where the final number is 73, that this is at least the same roll of film?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can conclude that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the picture number 58, you mentioned that those bodies had not been identified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, to my knowledge. If they had not been picked up at the morgue by the family, then generally they were not identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I please ask, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You are confronting the witness with -- that he said -- you say, "You mentioned that those bodies had not been identified." Could you please indicate where the witness has stated --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that in a document which is annexed to the internal reference number is 02 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where. If you refer to a statement by the witness you should be very precise where -- in an earlier statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor or that he testified in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to come to that, Mr. President, and I was going to give you the number. It is annex -- it is in an annex to his statement of the 29th of 30th of October and the 1st of November, 2001, which probably was done in The Hague, and the number is 25, and the internal reference number is 02129558.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. What exactly was said by Mr. Ashton in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means. I'm going to quote the second sentence in point 25.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] "I heard from the head of the State Hospital morgue that these two were not identified and were buried without the names." "Without the names." My question is the following: How is it possible -- how was it possible for you to get this information from the head of the morgue of the State Hospital, since you have just told us that this happened -- this photo was taken at the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. The head of the State Hospital and the head of the Kosevo Hospital were constantly travelling back and forth between the hospitals. I went with him down to the Kosevo Hospital when these bodies were taken down. And further on that, most bodies from State were taken to Kosevo because that's where most people would go to try to find the dead victim of their family. Now, I don't know if all the dead bodies from State Hospital were transferred to Kosevo Hospital, because some people did come to State Hospital to recover their dead family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I must go back to your previous statement, and I could look for it here, Mr. President, but I believe my memory, that it's quite good. At a certain point you mentioned an apartment block which was deliberately attacked and set alight, and you used the term "deliberately." Can you confirm that? It refers to your testimony before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that they were deliberately attacked, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you've reused this term "deliberately."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How are you in a position to know that it was a deliberate act?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when someone fires tank rounds repeatedly into a structure or into an area, but in this case the structure, for a period of time an occupied building, it would appear that, from my point of view on the ground, that this is a deliberate target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Have you ever heard that General Galic, who is on trial here, had deliberately given orders to shoot at that apartment block?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back to a point which I've just raised, because I have it at heart. We were talking about this iron cross, and I would just like to know whether you, with your own eyes, have ever seen any trace of such a cross anywhere at all in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not seen a trace of this iron cross in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm, sir, that when missiles hit the ground, missiles such as the one that you've referred to, they leave something that the technicians call a trace or a signature? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case you've referred to missiles. Yes, they do leave a trace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also confirm that the civil engineering structures and services in charge of repair work in Sarajevo at that stage were very limited, their abilities to do the repair work were very limited?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a consequence, if traces of the iron cross technique had been left on the ground, one would probably presumably have been in a position to spot them, because people would not have had the opportunity and time to repair the damage. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I arrived in Sarajevo in July, sir, and at that point there had been over 40.000 impacts in the streets and the buildings, so I would have no idea if it's been possible to trace a pattern. I mean, I would assume not because of the amount of damage by artillery. The destruction there was quite severe when I arrived, and continuing as I witnessed events. So I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Immediately following the attacks that you've photographed on the PTT building, you were still in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the attacks that I had the photographs presented earlier today as evidence? Yes, I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity in the days following that attack to visit the neighbourhood, the neighbourhood of the PTT building, that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I travelled around that neighbourhood, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me in saying that immediately after the attack you found no traces of the iron cross technique on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be impossible for me to say, because if somebody was doing such a technique, I wouldn't know how the traces would look. If they told me that they were doing this pattern -- I mean, I have no clue. No, I wouldn't be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? Why wouldn't you be able to see it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because when you -- because when you go outside of the building, the results of an impact are shrapnel, broken concrete, and debris?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. But if you were unable to see it, the others were unable to see it as well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've referred to the verb "to see." No one that I know -- I didn't mention in my testimony that I saw this particular pattern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you reply to my question, please. If you could not see it, others could not see it either, and that's going to be my penultimate question and then we'll be able to stop?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. No. I imagine not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this brings me to my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to intervene at this moment, because again the questioning is unclear. You can see something without recognising a pattern, because that's what you're talking about. So the question whether it's true or not that if you do not see something would implicate that someone else could not see either is not true. I'll give you an example. If you listen to Bach some people will identify certain structures in the music of Bach while others will just hear music. So your question is not correct, and therefore I interfere. I hope you'll keep this in mind and not continue on the false impression given by the question, that if Mr. Ashton didn't see something, that someone else could not see it either. And I may remind you that Mr. Ashton has testified in this court that only after he had shown photos, not just this photo, but other photos, it was explained to him that this was -- could be explained by the concept of an iron cross. That indicates that Mr. Ashton, at the time that he took the photographs - and your question was relating to the day after he took these photographs - might not have been aware of such a pattern, and like in the music of Bach might not have recognised by someone else, might not have done so. So it is giving a -- it is a misleading question, and I would like you not to continue on the basis of this question and the answer given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, does this mean that, in view of the time, I don't continue at all, or does it mean that I have to continue on a different basis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends. If you have one or two questions to put to the witness at this moment, you may proceed for a couple of minutes. I think I was quite clear about the basis of my interference -- intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under these circumstances, Mr. President, at what time do we need to conclude this afternoon, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have said ten minutes ago at 4.00, but it depends. We will finish at approximately 4.00, so I leave it up to you to find a suitable moment to end, for this moment, the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the appropriate time is now, and I'm going to continue with my cross-examination of the witness on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think this is not yet the moment to tender into evidence any of the photos or the maps, since the cross-examination of Mr. Ashton is still ongoing. I think the originals, especially those that are marked, should be in the hands of the Registry so that they can be used again next Monday. Madam Registrar, we start next Monday at I think it was 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'm writing you a note to remind you of that. Monday, next Monday, we're going to start at 9.00 in courtroom 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Courtroom 3, 9.00. We'll stay in recess until next Monday, 9.00. But Mr. Ierace wants to make an observation, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just two quick observations, Mr. President. First of all, the timetable indicates 9.15. Is it definitely 9.00 on Monday? utterances.text: Yes. I think we are in courtroom 3 next Monday, which solves our problem perhaps, but of course it needs some attention by the court management that those who will hear cases in this courtroom will have the profit of a working LiveNote as well. We'll pay attention to that, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And I just checked with the last updated courtroom calendar. Indeed, we're going to start at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that we have some new schedule. So 9.00 next Monday. We'll stay in recess until then.
